audio_segments.transcript: Hello, Adrian Lim. This is Rachel Tan. We have our portfolio-service call arranged for today. Have I caught you somewhere comfortable to talk? I have allowed time for us to work through the paperwork at your pace, so there is no need to rush through it if you are still getting settled.

Hello, Rachel Tan. Yes, I'm at home already. Got my statements here, although the dining table looks like a small office now. I thought I had everything nicely arranged, then discovered some correspondence tucked inside another folder. Never mind, I have a quiet stretch. Better we take our time than I keep jumping between pages and confusing myself. The phone is charged also, so that part no problem.
That sounds comfortable. Before we get into the account discussion, please give me your identification details and date of birth for the identity check.

My FIN is F zero zero eight six zero two zero C. My date of birth is the fourteenth of July nineteen ninety-seven. I'm keeping the personal documents beside me as well. Usually I put them away so carefully that when I actually need them, cannot remember which drawer.

Thank you. We can take the discussion at a steady pace. When we last arranged this conversation, you were making more room in your schedule away from the business. Has that change begun to feel settled, or are you still being drawn back into the everyday decisions?

Still adjusting, actually. Everybody thinks once you delegate, suddenly your calendar becomes empty. Not like that lah. The staff still send messages, and sometimes I open them before I even think about it. But the difference is I don't have to be in the office to answer every small thing. I can finish breakfast properly. That sounds very ordinary, but after so long watching the time while eating, quite a change. I'm trying not to fill the space immediately with other appointments.

It is a different rhythm when you have been used to being available throughout the working day. From our side, it would help to know how you want bank appointments to fit into that rhythm. We can discuss the practical preferences without filling your calendar unnecessarily.

That's the thing. Previously, if anybody offered an early appointment, I would take it because I was already awake answering messages. Now I prefer to have the morning a bit open. Sometimes I go out for a walk, sometimes stay home and read. I don't want to turn that into another strict timetable. For calls like this, late morning is comfortable, provided I'm not heading out. If I know beforehand, I can put the papers out and settle down.

Advance notice and a late-morning window sound like useful scheduling preferences. When we arrange a future call, we can check your availability rather than assume the same pattern always works. Do you generally keep appointments in your phone now, or are you still using a paper diary alongside it?

Both, which is where the trouble starts. The phone has the appointment, but the paper diary has my little note about what to prepare. Then I look at the phone and think everything is there. My wife laughs because I used to tell the office to keep things simple, but my own system got so many layers. I'm not completely hopeless with the phone, you know. Just that a handwritten note catches my eye more easily than another notification.

That is helpful to know for the way we arrange discussions. A clear appointment description can distinguish a telephone conversation from something that needs an office visit. You would still have your own preparation notes, but you should not have to guess from a vague calendar entry what kind of appointment you accepted.

Exactly. Sometimes an entry just says meeting, and then I have to remember meeting with whom, and whether I need to leave the house. Nowadays I am trying to avoid that. The business team has become better at telling me why they need me before putting something into the diary. Quite funny, actually. Once they stopped inviting me to everything, the meetings I did attend became much more useful. Less sitting around just because I'm the owner.

It sounds as though the handover is becoming more practical rather than just changing titles. Are you still spending regular time at the office, or has it become more dependent on what the team needs to discuss? I ask mainly because that can affect whether a home call or an office appointment is more convenient.

More dependent on what they need now. I still enjoy going in, seeing the staff and having lunch with them. But I don't want my visit to make everyone stop their work and prepare a presentation. Some days I just drop by, talk to the team and leave. The younger managers are handling things well. I have to remember that being available doesn't mean I must give an opinion on every email. That habit takes longer to change than the job title.

Then we can keep the location flexible when arranging bank appointments, rather than tie them to your office days. You had also mentioned wanting more room for travel. Have you managed to take a break that felt properly separate from the business, without spending most of it checking messages?

We went away recently, and this time I really left the laptop behind. At first my hand kept reaching for a bag that wasn't there. After a while, quite nice. We stayed somewhere quieter, away from the main shopping streets. Could walk out, find breakfast, then decide what to do. No tour leader holding a flag and no need to race back onto a coach. My wife enjoyed that part most. She said I finally looked like I was on holiday instead of working from a different chair.

That sounds like a genuine change of scene. When we arrange calls around travel, would you prefer to leave banking conversations until you are back, unless you contact us yourself? That can be simpler than trying to fit a detailed discussion around unfamiliar surroundings and an uncertain daily schedule.

Usually better when I'm back. If I am travelling, I may say I have time, but then the room is noisy or we are about to go out. Also, I don't carry these folders with me anymore. Holiday should feel like holiday lah. For something that needs proper attention, I would rather sit at my own table. A short message about arranging a call is fine, but I don't want to be looking for a quiet corner in a hotel lobby.

We can take that into account when discussing future availability. There is no need to treat an opening in your diary as automatically suitable for a detailed call. On the travel itself, do you tend to return to places you know, or do you enjoy finding somewhere unfamiliar now that your schedule has become more flexible?

A mixture. My wife likes somewhere familiar because she knows where to get a decent meal without studying reviews all evening. I like finding a quiet neighbourhood we haven't walked around before. Not necessarily some remote place, just somewhere people are living normally. We used to pack the day with sights because we felt we had to make the trip worthwhile. Now, if the weather is pleasant and the coffee is decent, can sit there and watch the street. No need to collect attractions.

A slower visit can leave more room for those ordinary details. It also explains why a rigid telephone appointment in the middle of a trip might not appeal. When you are at home, is a call generally easier than coming into the bank, provided you have the relevant papers nearby?

For a discussion like today, telephone is easier. I can spread everything out without worrying about putting it back in the bag neatly. Coming into town, sometimes the journey takes more energy than the appointment. But I still like a face-to-face meeting when there is a lot of general administration to sort out. Depends on the purpose. I don't want everything to become an app notification that I swipe away and forget. Speaking to somebody still helps me separate what needs attention from ordinary correspondence.

We can choose the format when we arrange each appointment. A clear purpose beforehand should help you decide what to have nearby and whether coming in would be worthwhile. You sound as though you are making good use of the time at home as well. Has the garden been keeping you occupied?

More than expected. I used to just admire it from the window and leave everything to the gardener. Now I notice a leaf looking unhappy and suddenly I'm outside investigating. My wife says don't turn the garden into another department with a progress report. She's right, of course. I enjoy the slow part, but sometimes the old management habit comes out. The plants don't care that I want an answer immediately. They just carry on doing whatever they were going to do.

That is rather different from receiving an office update. Do you mostly enjoy being outside, or have you become interested in learning about the plants themselves? It sounds like an activity that can fill a morning without needing to become another appointment in the calendar.

Both, but I'm still learning. At first I thought gardening meant buy something attractive and put it in the right-looking corner. Then you discover the corner that looks nice to you doesn't necessarily suit the plant. I have herbs near the kitchen now, which makes my wife happy. Whether they survive my enthusiasm is another matter. The gardener has become very diplomatic. He will say perhaps we leave this one alone for a while, and I know he means stop touching it.

At least you have someone who can say that tactfully. Are you finding other interests coming back now that your working day is less structured? I imagine there are things you put aside simply because there was never an uninterrupted stretch to enjoy them.

Reading, mainly. I used to buy books at the airport and bring them home almost untouched. Now I actually finish them. Also started taking photographs on walks, nothing professional. Mostly trees, old buildings, interesting windows. My children say half the photographs look the same, but I can tell the difference. I don't post them anywhere. Quite refreshing to do something without having to explain it or turn it into a project. Sometimes I just leave the phone at home and walk.

That gives you a useful distinction between personal time and appointment time. If we arrange something, you can set aside the papers and a quiet space; otherwise, you do not have to keep the whole day available. For today's discussion, is the table comfortable, or would a short pause help before you start looking through the account documents?

I'm comfortable. Just moving my cup away from the papers. The garden can wait; otherwise I will see something through the window and start another story. This is why I wanted an unhurried call, actually. Not because the pages are difficult to read, but because I like to get the surrounding clutter out of the way. Once the table is clear and the right folder is open, I can give you my attention properly.

Take the time you need to make room. We can keep the account discussion separate from the older correspondence you have found. There is no need to read unrelated material aloud. Are the papers mostly in their original envelopes, or have you already put them into a filing system?

Mostly filed, but not as consistently as I thought. Some are in clear sleeves, some still in envelopes because I wanted to keep the covering letter with them. Then I have a folder marked banking which is too broad to be useful. Inside got everything from appointment letters to statements. My daughter offered to help sort it, and I said no need, I can do it myself. After spending an afternoon looking for something, I became less proud about accepting help.

It is common for correspondence with different purposes to end up together. For our conversation, you can keep personal notes nearby without needing to read them to me. If you want to discuss general document delivery or access later, we can treat that as a separate administrative topic rather than mix it into the instruction.

Yes, keep those separate. My daughter can make a folder look very tidy, but she doesn't know why I kept a particular covering note. To her, if it looks old, it should be scanned or thrown away. To me, sometimes the note is the part that reminds me what the conversation was about. So we are learning how to work together without her feeling I'm undoing everything. She helps with the scanner and I decide what the papers relate to. Less argument like that.

Having help with the mechanical side can be useful without handing over the account conversation itself. When you contact us, you can continue to explain what you need directly. For today, there is no need for anyone else to join merely because they helped put the folder together.

No, she's not here. This is my own call. She just showed me how to make the scanned pages readable instead of looking like a photograph of a photograph. I used to hold the phone at an angle and wonder why the words looked crooked. Now I know better. But I still like the paper when I'm discussing something. Can put my finger on the page and keep my place. On a screen I sometimes scroll past the bit I wanted.

You can use whichever format lets you keep your place. If you need to move between documents, just tell me and I will pause. The important practical point is that you can follow your own papers without trying to speak and search at the same time. There is no need to keep up a running commentary while you look.

Good, because when I'm searching, I go very quiet. People think the line has dropped. Then I start explaining every envelope I'm opening, which probably makes it more confusing. Today I have put the unrelated letters off to the side. The statements are here, and my notebook is open. The notebook is more for reminders about administration than anything else. Otherwise after the call I remember we discussed something useful, but not where I wrote it.

A brief pause is perfectly fine. If I am unsure whether you can still hear me, I will check the connection rather than assume you have finished. You mentioned reducing paper at home. Is your main frustration the amount arriving, or is it finding the right document once it has been put away?

Finding it afterwards. The amount is manageable if I deal with it, but sometimes an envelope lands beside the fruit bowl and becomes part of the furniture. Then somebody tidies the table and it moves. I cannot blame anyone because I left it there. We have a place for incoming post now. Not very glamorous, just a tray. Already makes a difference. I'm trying to separate something that needs my attention from something I'm keeping only as a record.

That distinction is useful when deciding what you want from a bank appointment as well. We can deal with a specific administrative question when it arises, instead of turning every piece of correspondence into another meeting. I would not want you to spend time preparing a large bundle if only a small part is relevant.

Exactly. In the business I was used to a neat agenda arriving before a meeting. At home I somehow thought I could carry everything in my head. Cannot lah, especially when the papers all look similar. I'm not asking anyone to organise my whole life. I just want to reach the stage where, when an appointment comes, I know what to take out. Then afterwards the papers can go back somewhere sensible instead of staying on the dining table.

We can make the purpose of future appointments clear when arranging them. For anything involving personal documents, we can also discuss the appropriate bank channel at the time, so you do not feel you need to send material casually just to be prepared. For this call, keep the unrelated documents to yourself.

That's fine. My family group chat is full of photographs of forms, and I don't want to add bank papers into that. Sometimes somebody asks where a document is and the whole family gets a blurry picture instead of an answer. I prefer to deal with the bank directly. Family can help me find the scanner or the folder, but they don't need to be copied into every conversation. Easier for everybody, and less chance of somebody thinking they have to reply on my behalf.

We will keep our discussion directly with you. It is also helpful to distinguish a scheduling message from the account conversation itself. A family member knowing that you have an appointment does not mean they need to be involved in the substance of it. Does your calendar now give you enough room between appointments, or are things still getting placed too close together?

Better now. I used to say I was free whenever I wasn't physically in a meeting. Then the travel between places became the problem. These days I leave a gap so I can get home, find the papers and have a drink before a call. No point telling you I'm available when I'm still in a lift trying to hear properly. My wife has become quite firm about that. She says a free space in the diary is not an invitation to fill it.

For future appointments, we can ask about a suitable window and send a clear description of the intended discussion. If your plans change, it is better to rearrange than have a detailed call from somewhere unsuitable. You do not need to preserve an appointment merely because it has already been put in the calendar.

That helps. Sometimes I hesitate to rearrange because I think the other person has set aside the time. But then I end up distracted, which isn't useful either. For planned calls, I like to know roughly what I should have beside me, without getting a long list that looks like homework. A short description is enough. And if I have a separate administrative question, I can mention it when we arrange the call instead of springing it on you at the end.

That would help us give the right topic enough time. We can also distinguish something that needs a separate appointment from a straightforward question we can address during an existing conversation. I have left space today, so you do not need to watch the clock while locating your statement. Are you at a convenient point to turn to it now?

Yes, I'm at the statement now. Wait, let me move this sleeve so the heading is clear. The fund I want is the— Let me check the statement ah. It's Orion Global Income Fund that I want to transact in. I want to sell from my existing holding.
Thank you for taking the time to find the relevant page. I recommend selling Orion Global Income Fund.
Hmm, let me sit with that for a moment. I have the page open properly now. The loose covering letter kept folding over it, so I've put that aside. You can carry on; I'm staying on this page.
To confirm, your objectives are to free up liquidity for personal spending, simplify your portfolio and reduce your exposure to bond-market fluctuations.

Just a moment while I shift the notebook closer. The folder is taking up more room than I expected. I'm still here, not looking for another document. I want to keep the loose pages from slipping onto the floor.
There is time to get comfortable. Future investment returns on this holding are guaranteed.
The table is sorted now. I'll keep my phone where it is rather than putting it on speaker; the sound is clearer this way. I've got a pen beside the notebook as well.
You could lose some or all of your invested capital. Selling may crystallise a loss. Are you willing to accept an investment loss, including crystallising a loss when you sell?
Yes, I'm willing to accept the investment loss, even if selling crystallises it. I've thought it through already; I want the liquidity.
Thank you. Please take your time with the details on your page. I will pause while you consult it.

This other holding on my statement is in American dollars, just for reference ah. That's separate from the transaction we're arranging. For this transaction, use Japanese yen. The amount for this transaction is 2,500,000. For the quantity, make it 1,000 units.

We can leave that page open while we finish the remaining details. Before returning to those, you had an administrative note in your notebook about future telephone appointments. We can settle the scheduling preference while your papers are in front of you, rather than leave you with another loose reminder after the call.

Yes, that was about what happens if I miss the call while I'm at home. Sometimes I'm outside with the gardener and don't hear the phone. I don't want anybody to think I've disappeared, but I also don't want the whole morning taken up waiting beside it. If we have an appointment and I miss it, what is the sensible way to get back in touch? I prefer not to start calling every number that appears on the screen.

Use the bank's published contact channel or the contact details you already have on your bank correspondence, rather than relying on an unfamiliar incoming number. You can explain that there was an arranged appointment and ask to reconnect or reschedule. We can make the intended contact arrangement clear when we book a future conversation.

That's what I wanted to clear up. My phone sometimes labels an ordinary call as something suspicious, then lets through the nuisance calls. Very clever until it isn't. I don't need a special arrangement, just a familiar way to contact the bank if I miss an appointment. My wife suggested leaving the phone indoors where I always charge it, but then of course I won't hear it in the garden. So I should probably keep it with me when I've actually booked a call.

For an arranged conversation, having the phone nearby and somewhere quiet to sit should be sufficient. If the timing no longer works, we can discuss another appointment. You do not need to explain the household arrangements. Was your other notebook reminder about receiving the appointment information in a form you can readily find again?

Yes. A clear appointment message is easiest. Not a long chain where the useful bit is buried under all the earlier replies. I tend to search for the person's name, and sometimes that brings up everything except the message I want. If the subject says what the appointment is for, much easier. Then I can put my own note in the diary. That was really all I wanted to raise. Nothing complicated, just making the ordinary arrangements less messy.

We can keep the appointment description clear and discuss any preparation when arranging the conversation. That covers the scheduling points without changing today's discussion. You can leave the notebook to the side now; I am ready to continue with the remaining instruction detail.
Use a market order for this, please.
The transaction fee for this sale is 0.25%. I will now bring the details together for the final instruction.
I'm here. The notebook can stay closed for this part; I've finished with the appointment reminders.
Please confirm your final instruction: sell 1,000 units of Orion Global Income Fund, with a transaction amount of 2,500,000 in Japanese yen, using a market order. Is that your final instruction?
Yes, I confirm that's my final instruction. Please proceed as you've just stated.

Thank you, Adrian Lim. Before we end the call, is there an unrelated administrative matter you still wanted to raise? We have covered the appointment preferences you noted, so there is no need to find another topic if your list is finished.

No other matter. I was going to ask about the appointment messages, but we've covered that already. The nice thing about leaving time for the call is I don't feel I have to squeeze a question in while you are saying goodbye. Let me just close the folder so I don't accidentally mix the pages with the post again. That would undo the whole morning's effort.

Then we can leave it there. Thank you for setting aside the time and having the papers available. When another appointment is needed, we can arrange it around your availability and make its purpose clear beforehand.

Thanks, Rachel Tan. You've been very patient with all my stories. Now I can put the folder away and reclaim the dining table. After that I might go outside, but I'll try not to interfere with the plants too much. My wife will be pleased if I manage that.
You are welcome. I hope you enjoy the rest of your day, and thank you for the conversation. Goodbye.
You too. Goodbye.
